Don't Laugh: The Maxi-Scooter Is a Serious Tourer

Mention touring on a scooter and you will get a few raised eyebrows. Then people ride a modern maxi-scooter and the smirk vanishes. Machines like the Honda Forza 750 pair proper motorcycle performance with the effortless convenience of twist-and-go, generous weather protection and built-in storage. Across Europe, maxi-scooters are a common sight loaded up for two-week tours, and in the UK they make brilliant sense for a rider who wants distance without complication. Here is how to make the most of one.

The Twist-and-Go Advantage

The single biggest touring benefit of a maxi-scooter is the automatic transmission. On a long day, especially through stop-start traffic getting out of a city or grinding up a busy A-road, the absence of a clutch and gear changes is a genuine relief. Your left hand rests, your left foot relaxes, and you simply steer, brake and enjoy the view. On flowing routes like the A82 through Glencoe or the sweeping Welsh A5, the automatic gearbox lets you focus entirely on your lines and the scenery. Fatigue over a long touring day is noticeably lower than on a manual bike.

The convenience of twist-and-go is not a gimmick. On a 300-mile day it genuinely reduces fatigue and lets you concentrate on the road and the view rather than clutch and gears.

Luggage: Storage Built In

Maxi-scooters start with a huge advantage: the underseat storage. Most will swallow a full-face helmet plus a surprising amount of soft kit, all locked away and weatherproof. For touring you simply add capacity on top. A Givi V47 Monokey Top Box bolts onto the rear rack, adds a passenger backrest and gives you a secure home for a second helmet and your daily essentials. Combined with the underseat compartment, that is enough storage for a solo week away without a single strap or bungee. For heavier loads or two-up trips you can add side cases, and our luggage mounting guide covers fitting them correctly.

Wind Protection: Already Good, Easily Great

Maxi-scooters come with far more standard weather protection than most motorcycles. The large front fairing and screen keep rain and wind off your legs and torso, which is a revelation on a wet British day. The stock screen is usually a good starting point, but for taller riders it can leave the airflow hitting your helmet. An adjustable screen such as the Givi Airflow Adjustable Screen lets you dial in the perfect height for motorway cruising. Getting the screen top just below your line of sight is the goal, and our motorcycle windscreen guide explains exactly how to judge it.

Comfort and Ergonomics

The relaxed, feet-forward or feet-down riding position of a maxi-scooter is naturally comfortable, and the seats tend to be broad and well-padded, closer to an armchair than a motorcycle perch. The floorboards let you shift your feet around to stave off stiffness on a long haul. To finish the touring setup I add:

  • Heated grips if not fitted as standard. Oxford Heaterz Premium Heated Grips take the sting out of a chilly morning over the Cat and Fiddle.
  • A phone mount. The wide handlebar area suits a Quad Lock Motorcycle Mount perfectly for sat-nav.
  • An intercom. A Cardo Packtalk Edge Intercom makes navigation prompts and music seamless on the relaxed rides these machines encourage.

Range and Fuel Strategy

Larger maxi-scooters carry decent-sized tanks and their efficient engines deliver strong economy, so real-world range is often comparable to a mid-size motorcycle. A Forza 750 will comfortably see well over 150 miles between fills at a touring pace. That is more than enough for most UK touring, but the usual Highland rule applies on the remote sections of the NC500: top up whenever you pass a station rather than gambling on the next one being open. Ridden smoothly, a maxi-scooter is one of the most economical ways to cover big distances.

Pace and Route Planning

A modern maxi-scooter with a 750cc engine has genuine performance and will happily cruise at motorway speeds all day and overtake with confidence. That said, these are machines that reward a smooth, flowing style rather than aggressive corner-carving. They are superb on sweeping A-roads and relaxed touring routes, and the low centre of gravity makes them wonderfully easy to manage in towns and at fuel stops. Plan days that mix scenic A-roads with the odd motorway transit and a maxi-scooter will handle both without complaint. Tighter, more technical roads like Bealach na Ba are perfectly doable, just taken at a measured pace.

What to Upgrade First

Because maxi-scooters arrive so well-equipped, the upgrade list is short. Add a top box for extra storage, an adjustable screen if you are tall, and heated grips if they are not standard. That is genuinely most of what you need, which is a big part of the appeal and the value.

Honest Limitations

A maxi-scooter is not the bike for spirited backroad scratching, and the automatic transmission, while relaxing, removes some of the engagement that manual riders love. Ground clearance is lower than a conventional motorcycle, and the sheer practicality can feel a touch clinical to riders who crave drama. Two-up touring is comfortable but check pillion legroom, and our pillion touring guide has advice on setting the bike up for a passenger.

Who It Suits

Maxi-scooter touring suits the pragmatic rider who prizes comfort, weather protection, storage and easy, fatigue-free progress over outright thrills. It is ideal for commuters who also want to tour, for riders returning to two wheels who want simplicity, and for anyone who values arriving relaxed. A machine like the Honda Forza 750 blurs the line between scooter and motorcycle so thoroughly that once you have toured on one, you may never look at a manual bike the same way again. Do not let anyone talk you out of it: for stress-free distance riding, the humble maxi-scooter is one of touring's best-kept secrets.
